subject: Copywriting
title: EXTRA! EXTRA! The Art of the Scream
description: A micro-lesson that makes EXTRA! EXTRA! The Art of the Scream usable.

hook.text: 'DEWEY DEFEATS TRUMAN'—the most famous wrong headline ever. Printed in 1948, wrong by morning.

buildup.text: Newspaper headlines had to sell on newsstands. They competed with every other paper on the rack.

discovery.text: Tabloids mastered the art: big type, punchy verbs, emotional words. 'HEADLESS BODY IN TOPLESS BAR' is legend.

twist.text: Broadsheets considered tabloid headlines beneath them. But readers bought tabloids. Attention beats dignity.

climax.text: The New York Post's headline writers became celebrities. Their front pages were shared like memes, decades early.

punchline.text: Sell papers in six words. Tabloids wrote the playbook.

quiz.question: What made the 'DEWEY DEFEATS TRUMAN' headline famous?

details.summary: Newspaper hawkers once shouted 'Extra! Extra!' to sell breaking news on street corners. This tradition of the 'screamer headline' — bold, urgent, impossible to ignore — defined newspaper sales for over a century. The art of the scream evolved into tabloid headlines, push notifications, and...
details.whyItMatters: The screamer headline tradition reveals that urgency has always been the most powerful driver of news consumption. Understanding its evolution helps writers calibrate urgency across modern channels.
takeaways: Screamer headlines drove newspaper sales through urgency and spectacle
The tradition evolved from street hawkers to tabloid front pages
Modern push notifications are the digital equivalent of 'Extra! Extra!'

faq.question: What made screamer headlines effective for selling newspapers?
faq.answer: They created instant urgency in a crowded street. A bold, shocking statement demanded immediate action — buy the paper now or miss the story. This time-sensitivity and emotional impact are the same principles that drive effective push notifications today.

faq.question: When did screamer headlines fall out of use?
faq.answer: As radio and television delivered breaking news faster than print, the need for Extra editions declined. But the screamer aesthetic survived in tabloid journalism and has evolved into breaking news banners, push notifications, and social media alerts.
